title: Spectral selection and repulsion
subtitle: G2 lecture 119000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: A spectral gap tells us where an operator has no spectrum.
body: An off-diagonal perturbation does something stronger: under the right block-order hypothesis, it cannot push spectral values into the original gap at all. The gap is repelled, and its endpoints provide a canonical way to choose the perturbed subspace. This is the starting point of Davis and Kahan's Theorem eight point one. We will derive the gap protection, identify the selected reducing branch, and explain the cosine factors in the theorem's stronger comparisons.

slides.title: Build the two-block setting
body: Decompose the Hilbert space orthogonally into a subspace P and its perpendicular complement. Suppose P reduces A, so A is block diagonal relative to this decomposition. Assume the spectrum of the first block is at most alpha, while the spectrum of the second block is at least alpha plus delta, where delta is positive. We call P the low subspace and its complement the high subspace. Let H be self-adjoint and off-diagonal: both diagonal compressions of H vanish. In block-matrix form, H has zeros on the diagonal and an operator B in the lower-left corner, with B adjoint in the upper-right corner. Define S to be A plus H.

slides.title: Prove the spectral gap survives
slides.lead: Choose any real number lambda strictly between alpha and alpha plus delta.
body: We want to prove S minus lambda times the identity is invertible. In a finite-dimensional model, write its diagonal blocks as A low minus lambda and A high minus lambda. The first is strictly negative, and the second strictly positive. Suppose S has an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda. Write it as a pair x and y in the low and high subspaces. The eigenvalue equations say that A low minus lambda applied to x plus B adjoint applied to y is zero, and B applied to x plus A high minus lambda applied to y is zero. Take the inner product of the first equation with x and of the second with y.

slides.title: See the effect in a plane
slides.lead: Let A have diagonal entries negative one and one.
body: The gap is the open interval from negative one to one. Add an off-diagonal symmetric perturbation whose two off-diagonal entries are h. The eigenvalues of S are negative and positive square root of one plus h squared. Both move away from zero as h increases. Neither can enter the original gap. For h equal to three, they become approximately negative three point one six two and positive three point one six two. The new low eigenspace rotates, but the gap itself remains protected, no matter how large h becomes. This phenomenon is often called spectral repulsion. A diagonal perturbation would destroy the argument.

slides.title: Select the canonical branch
slides.lead: Since S has no spectrum in the open gap, define Q as its spectral subspace for eigenvalues at most alpha.
body: In a finite-dimensional matrix, Q is the span of all eigenvectors with eigenvalues at most alpha. In Hilbert space it is the range of the bounded Borel spectral projection for the half-line ending at alpha. This definition has no arbitrary eigenbasis or angle choices. The spectral repulsion result shows that the complementary subspace automatically has spectrum at least alpha plus delta. Q and its complement reduce S. Theorem eight point one goes further: the maximal angle between P and this Q is strictly below forty-five degrees.

slides.title: Recover the block compression inequality
slides.lead: Why do cosines of principal angles appear in Theorem eight point one's later parts?
body: Decompose the original high subspace using the new low and high spectral projections of S. Write C for the overlap from the original high subspace into the new high subspace. The complementary overlap goes into the new low subspace. Since the original high compression of H is zero, compressing S to the original high subspace gives exactly the original high block of A. Subtract alpha from the corresponding quadratic form. On the new low spectral component, S minus alpha is nonpositive. Dropping that contribution can only increase the form.

slides.title: From forms to eigenvalue comparisons
slides.lead: In finite dimensions, order of positive self-adjoint matrices implies order of their decreasing eigenvalue sequences by Courant–Fischer.
body: Applying this principle to the compression inequality gives repulsion estimates for ordered eigenvalues, with cosine factors. The source also proves dimension-free approximation-number formulations and finite-dimensional inequalities for symmetric gauges. Those conclusions require an additional step: comparing positive compressed operators at the level of singular-value prefixes, then passing from weak majorization to each supported symmetric gauge.

slides.title: The role of the quarter angle
slides.lead: In the two-by-two model, the low eigenvector of S is rotated from the old low axis by theta satisfying tangent twice theta equal to the magnitude of h.
body: This always puts theta below forty-five degrees. As h tends to infinity, the angle approaches forty-five degrees from below. So the strict threshold does not imply that the subspaces remain extremely close for a large perturbation. It asserts that the canonical low branch cannot exchange roles with the high branch. That is exactly the information a doubled-sine estimate lacks.

slides.title: Why dimensions and defects still matter
slides.lead: For finite-dimensional P and Q, the low spectral branch has the same rank as P.
body: A continuous deformation from zero coupling is one way to see this; the spectral-gap argument prevents an eigenvalue from crossing the separating threshold. In infinite dimensions, equal cardinal dimensions do not force the two directed projection gaps to agree. A full symmetric-angle statement needs additional compatibility of the crossed defects or suitable finite-dimensional hypotheses. Otherwise retain the directed conclusion.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: We now have a concrete mechanism for identifying the intended spectral subspace: form-separated diagonal blocks plus an off-diagonal self-adjoint perturbation preserve the open gap, define a canonical spectral projection, and keep the selected branch below a quarter turn.
body: The compression identities then yield the eigenvalue and norm inequalities. It allows more general perturbations, but demands quantitative smallness relative to a spectral gap. We will show how that smallness can certify the correct angular branch.
